system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2153-12-17 14:56:00 to 2153-12-18 16:08:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease with prior amputations, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for cough, nausea, and nocturnal hypoxia. His blood pressure was elevated on presentation but improved with medication. He was found to have oxygen desaturation during sleep, consistent with his known sleep apnea, which he had not been treating due to CPAP discomfort. A plan was made with the sleep team to initiate nocturnal home oxygen at 3 liters per minute instead of PAP therapy, given concern for complex sleep apnea. His kidney function remained stable, tacrolimus levels were therapeutic, and his other chronic conditions were managed without change. He was discharged home the following day with arranged oxygen delivery and plans for outpatient follow-up with sleep and nephrology specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you've been having a lot of back pain lately. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been going on for about three months, but it’s gotten much worse in the past few weeks. It’s a burning pain, right here—about two inches left of my spine in the middle of my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does it go anywhere else? Like down your legs or around your side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It spreads out toward my side, almost to my armpit. But it doesn’t get worse when I move or breathe deeply. No rash either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you said it’s not helped by Tylenol or lidocaine patches anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing’s helping. I couldn’t even sleep last night. I was up till 5 a.m. just trying to get comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been through that. We’ve also noted you’ve had abdominal pain too. Can you describe that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been there for about a month. It’s usually in my lower left side, but now it’s more in the middle. Feels like gurgling, and sometimes it goes into my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any changes in bowel movements or bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bowel movements are normal, but I do feel bloated a lot. My GI doctor ran tests—colonoscopy, MRI—but didn’t find anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. But your GI doctor mentioned your stool tests came back showing pancreatic insufficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreatic what? I’ve never heard of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means your pancreas isn’t making enough enzymes to help digest food, especially fats. That can cause bloating and discomfort after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I feel so full and gassy? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. We’re going to start you on a medication called Creon. It’s a digestive enzyme you take with meals to help your body break down food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my back pain? Any idea what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest MRI yesterday to check for serious causes like aortic dissection, especially given your history. Good news—it ruled that out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what about the pain itself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI didn’t show any fractures or tumors. Today we did a spine X-ray, which also looked normal. So it’s likely musculoskeletal—maybe muscle spasm or strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no nerve damage or herniated disc?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. You don’t have weakness, numbness, or bowel/bladder issues, which are red flags. So we’re not concerned about spinal cord involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. So what’s the plan for the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your acetaminophen to 1000 mg three times a day. We’re also adding a muscle relaxant called tizanidine, three times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. So we suggest taking the first dose at night. Don’t drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other medicines—am I still taking those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your usual meds—insulin, blood pressure pills, tacrolimus, and the rest—are continuing. Your kidney function is stable, and your tacrolimus level was in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My creatinine’s been going up lately though—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has been slowly rising, which we’re monitoring. But it didn’t change during this stay. The transplant team is aware and will follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And the Creon—how do I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three capsules with each meal. It helps break down food so your body can absorb nutrients better and reduce bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your GI doctor will reassess over time. For now, it’s important to manage your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. The new meds seem to be helping a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, and we’ve addressed the main issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I just keep taking the new meds and follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep up with your PCP for the back pain and GI for the pancreatic insufficiency. We’ll send all the info to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney and transplant team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re updated. Continue all your immunosuppressants and insulin as prescribed. Watch for any signs of infection or rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks, doctor. I feel better knowing we have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your prescriptions ready, and you should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to get some rest in my own bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Use the pain meds as directed, and don’t hesitate to call if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for worsening chronic back pain and abdominal discomfort. His back pain, described as a constant burning sensation in the mid-thoracic region, was evaluated with imaging including a chest MRA and thoracic spine X-ray, both of which showed no acute abnormalities. The pain was deemed likely musculoskeletal, and his pain regimen was optimized with increased acetaminophen and addition of tizanidine. Abdominal bloating and pain were attributed to newly diagnosed pancreatic insufficiency, confirmed by stool testing, and he was started on Creon. His kidney function remained stable, immunosuppressive and chronic disease medications were continued, and he was discharged home with follow-up arranged with his primary care provider and gastroenterologist.
